attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay; not a quote of anyone else.

semantics.note: Keeps all three parts: massive loss, no owned infrastructure, no path to profit beyond spending others' money. Dropping 'training' does not matter. The profitability part is partly evaluative but is stated as present fact.

contract.note: Reading the loss as the company-wide 2025 operating loss (tied to the $21B in context), and infrastructure as owned physical compute, is an ordinary plain reading. 'No path' read as no credible operating route is fair. The result depends on these readings.

evidence.note: Reports a 2025 operating loss of $20.92B on $13.07B revenue, from audited statements. That is a substantial operating loss. It also notes management hopes for profit by 2030, which is only a forecast.
January 2026 CFO disclosure: 'partnering rather than owning'. This supports reliance on others' infrastructure. It is a company disclosure and is not an ownership register.
OpenAI was an announced equity funder in Stargate. That makes an absolute no-ownership claim less clean, but it does not show OpenAI owned operating assets.
April 2026 report, citing the FT, that OpenAI prefers long-term leases and that SoftBank owns the Abilene site. This supports the claim that it does not own its infrastructure.

reviews.rationale: Two parts hold. The 2025 operating loss was large relative to revenue (e1), and OpenAI relied on partners' and leased infrastructure (e2, e4); the Stargate equity in e3 does not show it owned operating assets. The third part is unsettled: the packet has no complete operating model showing that no credible route to profit exists, and the 2030 target is only a management forecast. So part is supported and the profitability-path part is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Correctly identifies OpenAI and Anthropic and keeps both the promotional activity and the claimed investor-facing purpose. Calling it causal fits, because the core is the motive behind the giveaways.

contract.note: Requires dated promotions for both firms plus evidence of the investor-facing purpose. Reading 'effectively paying' as subsidy is fair. Treating motive as a separate component is a reasonable reading of the sentence.

evidence.note: February 2026 OpenAI announcement of free Codex access for a limited time. This supports the promotion part for OpenAI only. It shows no API credits, no status in June, and no motive.
March 2026 report of doubled Claude usage for two weeks. It shows a promotional pattern, but it is not API credits or free weeks of paid access, and it says nothing about investor motive.

reviews.rationale: The packet partly supports the promotion part: OpenAI offered free Codex access (e1) and Anthropic offered extra usage (e2). Nothing in the packet establishes the claimed purpose of impressing VCs and public markets, and the exact credits/free-weeks combination near publication is not documented. Nothing contradicts the claim either. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, restating his own earlier reporting.

semantics.note: Keeps the $8.67B figure and the January–September 2025 period. It leaves out the claim that the FT verified the figure and adds the profitability rebuttal implied by context. Acceptable overall.

contract.note: Requires independent corroboration of the figure, matching its scope. Treating the speaker's own reporting as unable to prove itself is correct under policy. The contract is fair.

evidence.note: November 2025 TechCrunch repeats Zitron's analysis (~$8.65B for nine months). It attributes the figure to him and does not independently verify it.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence repeats the speaker's own figure, so it cannot verify the figure. The FT article could not be read, and there are no underlying records or reconciliation. Nothing establishes a different amount. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Keeps the exclusive 'entirely' claim and the claimed sequence from price change to ROI complaints. The language is heavily rhetorical, but the causal core is firm.

contract.note: Reading 'entirely' as exclusive is faithful to the firm wording. 'Actual costs' is undefined, so the contract requires a cost-covering price, which is a reasonable plain reading. The result depends on these readings.

evidence.note: Randomised study: productivity information raised AI adoption, but only among firms with high decision authority. It covers AI broadly, not generative tools at full price. That is suggestive, not decisive, for an independent adoption driver.

June 2026: Anthropic paused SDK billing at API rates as it was due to take effect. The cost increase was never charged, and API rates are not shown to equal actual costs. This neither establishes nor refutes the claimed sequence.

reviews.rationale: e1 hints that productivity beliefs also drive adoption, but its scope (AI broadly, one subgroup) does not establish an independent driver for the generative-AI products in context. e2 shows no cost-covering price was actually charged. Nothing settles either the exclusive causal claim or the pricing-response sequence. Unresolved.
